title: What is the difference between compiled and interpreted languages?
description: Understand the fundamental difference between compilation and interpretation.

data.text: **Question:** What is the difference between compiled and interpreted languages?

Compiled languages convert source code into machine code before execution, resulting in faster runtime performance. Interpreted languages translate code line-by-line during execution, offering more flexibility and cross-platform compatibility but slower performance.

**Compiled Languages:**
- Source code is converted to machine code (binary) by a compiler before execution
- The compilation step happens once, producing an executable file
- Runtime execution is very fast since the code is already in machine language
- Examples: C, C++, Rust, Go
- Platform-specific: compiled binaries run only on the target platform
- Debugging can be harder as errors are caught at compile-time

**Interpreted Languages:**
- Source code is read and executed line-by-line by an interpreter
- No separate compilation step needed
- Slower execution due to runtime translation
- Examples: Python, JavaScript, Ruby
- Platform-independent: code runs anywhere with the interpreter
- Easier to debug as errors are caught at runtime

**Hybrid Approach:**
- Modern languages use a hybrid approach
- Java compiles to bytecode, then JVM interprets/JIT compiles it
- C# compiles to IL, then CLR executes it
- This provides both portability and performance

Interviewers want to assess:
- Understanding of how code executes at a fundamental level
- Awareness of performance trade-offs
- Knowledge of modern hybrid approaches
- Ability to choose the right language for a use case

points: Compiled languages convert to machine code before execution
Trade-offs exist between performance and portability
data.takeaway: Understanding compilation vs interpretation helps in choosing the right tool and optimizing performance.
